families.label: k-t-b
families.contrast: The writing family is shared, but the everyday word for book differs: Arabic kitāb and Syriac kṯāḇā belong here; Hebrew sefer belongs to s-p-r. A shared concept does not require a shared root.

usage.ar: Current standard Arabic: kataba means wrote; kitāb is a book. Spoken dialects have their own pronunciation and inflection.
usage.he: Modern Hebrew: katav means wrote; mikhtav is a written letter. The ordinary noun book is sefer, from another root.
usage.syc: Classical Syriac: writing and books. A modern Assyrian Neo-Aramaic book continuation is documented on the linked entry; its pronunciation is not the Classical Syriac pronunciation.

families.label: ʿ-b-d
families.summary: Service, work and doing — meanings diverge
families.contrast: Do not translate this root with one universal English word. Arabic ʿabada commonly concerns worship or service; Hebrew avad is everyday work or functioning; Classical Syriac ʿbad includes doing and making. Arabic everyday work is commonly expressed by ʿ-m-l instead.

usage.ar: Current standard Arabic: ʿibāda is worship, maʿbad a place of worship. The root is not a general replacement for every English use of work.
usage.he: Modern Hebrew: avad means worked and can describe a device functioning; avoda means work or a job. Other constructions have additional meanings.
usage.syc: Classical Syriac: do, make, work and service. Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ʿāḇēḏ still means do or make; this is a separately labelled modern variety, not a Classical conjugation.

links.gloss: to do, to make, to work

families.label: s-p-r / s-f-r
families.summary: Counting, telling, books — and Arabic travel
families.contrast: These consonant correspondences do not make every sense identical. Hebrew safar is count, siper tell, sefer book; the haircut/barber branch is a separate sense history. Syriac has writing, books and scribes. Arabic safar is travel; sifr can mean a book or volume. Arabic kitāb comes from k-t-b. Keep the independent senses apart.

usage.ar: Current standard Arabic: sāfara means travel. Book/volume sifr is a literary term; ordinary kitāb belongs to k-t-b.
usage.he: Modern Hebrew: sefer book, safar counted, siper told. Identical unpointed letters may also represent a barber; vowels and context matter.
usage.syc: Classical Syriac records books, writing and scribes, alongside distinct homographs. No family-wide claim about modern spoken usage is verified here.

families.label: ṣ-l-ḥ
families.contrast: Arabic ṣ-l-ḥ includes being sound or suitable and repairing/reforming. Hebrew ts-l-ḥ includes crossing and succeeding, with hitsliakh meaning succeeded. Syriac ṣlaḥ means prosper or succeed. This is ṣ/ts and ḥ/kh, not plain s and h; ASCII search accepts s l h as a convenience, not a historical identity rule.

usage.ar: Current standard Arabic: aṣlaḥa means repaired or improved; ṣulḥ is reconciliation. These senses should not be substituted for Hebrew succeed without context.
usage.he: Modern Hebrew: hitsliakh succeeded, hatslakha success. The paʿal verb also has a crossing/traversing sense.
usage.syc: Classical Syriac: prosper or succeed. Modern spoken continuation is not verified in this pack.

families.label: k-l-b

excludedLinks.gloss: An ant of the genus Atta.

families.contrast: Arabic kalb, Hebrew kelev and Syriac kalbā share the dog word. A family can also contain extended meanings and homographs; those are not synonyms for dog. The native words and their independent dictionary senses appear below.

usage.ar: Kalb is the ordinary standard Arabic dog word. Some figurative uses are insults; the animal sense is the learning default.
usage.he: Kelev is the ordinary Modern Hebrew dog word; kalba is the feminine form. Use context to separate neutral animal references from insults.
usage.syc: Classical kalbā means dog. The linked source also documents dog in Assyrian Neo-Aramaic and Turoyo; their vowels and pronunciation differ by variety.

families.label: sh-l-m / s-l-m
families.contrast: Arabic salām, Hebrew shalom and Syriac shlāma illustrate a documented s/sh correspondence. The family includes completeness and well-being, but its other derived words keep their own meanings.

usage.ar: Salām is peace and occurs in greeting expressions in standard Arabic and spoken varieties.
usage.he: Shalom is peace and is used as a greeting in Modern Hebrew.
usage.syc: Shlāma is peace and well-being in Classical Syriac. Contemporary liturgical use does not by itself establish a particular modern spoken dialect.
